title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The fundamental, essential meaning of the European events of the early nineteenth century lies in the movement of the mass of European peoples from west to east, and afterward from east to west. The movement from west to east came first. For the peoples of the west to be able to make their warlike march all the way to Moscow, three things had to happen: (1) they had to form themselves into a military group of a size large enough to withstand a collision with the warlike military group of the east; (2) they had to throw off all their established traditions and customs; and (3) during their military march they had to have at their head a man who could justify to himself, and to them, the lies, the robberies, and the murders that this march would require.

And starting with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately sized group was broken apart, along with the old habits and traditions, and step by step a new group was formed, larger in scale, with new customs and new traditions, and a man was produced who could stand at the head of the coming march and carry the responsibility for everything it would take.

A man with no convictions, no habits, no traditions, not even a name of his own, not even a Frenchman, emerges—by what look like the strangest chances—from the whole seething mass of French factions, and without attaching himself to any one of them, is carried forward into a position of prominence.

The ignorance of his colleagues, the weakness and insignificance of his opponents, the sheer bluntness of his lies, and this man's dazzling, self-assured limitations, all combine to raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant qualities of the soldiers sent to Italy, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish daring and self-confidence win him military fame. Countless so-called chances follow him wherever he goes. Falling out of favor with the rulers of France turns to his advantage. His attempts to escape his predestined path all fail: he is refused a place in the Russian service, and the post he seeks in Turkey comes to nothing. During the war in Italy he comes to the brink of destruction several times, and each time is saved in some unexpected way. And thanks to various diplomatic considerations, the Russian armies—the very ones that might have destroyed his reputation—never turn up on the scene until he is already gone.

When he comes back from Italy he finds the government in Paris in the middle of falling apart—a process in which everyone attached to it is inevitably swept away and destroyed. And by chance, a way out of this dangerous position presents itself, in the form of a pointless, senseless expedition to Africa. Once again so-called chance goes with him. Impregnable Malta surrenders without a single shot fired. His most reckless schemes come off brilliantly. The enemy fleet, which afterward would not let a single boat slip past, lets his entire army through unharmed. In Africa a whole series of outrages are committed against a nearly defenseless population. And the men who commit these crimes, above all their leader, convince themselves that this is admirable, that this is glory—it resembles Caesar, it resembles Alexander the Great, and so it must be good.

This ideal of glory and grandeur—which consists not merely in seeing nothing wrong in whatever one does, but in actually taking pride in every crime one commits, treating it as if it carried some incomprehensible, almost supernatural meaning—this ideal, which would go on to guide this man and everyone around him, found room to develop in Africa. Whatever he attempts succeeds. The plague does not touch him. The cruelty of murdering prisoners is never held against him as a fault. His childish, reckless, needless, and shameful departure from Africa, abandoning his own comrades in the middle of their troubles, is chalked up to his credit, and once again the enemy fleet lets him slip past, not once but twice. And when, drunk on the crimes he has carried off so successfully, he reaches Paris, the collapse of the republican government—which a year earlier might have finished him—has now gone as far as it can go, and his arrival there, a newcomer with no ties to any faction, can only lift him higher still. And though he himself has no plan of his own, he is more than ready to step into his new role.
He had no plan, he was afraid of everything, but the factions snatched at him and demanded that he take part.

He alone—armed with his ideal of glory and grandeur, worked out in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime, his bluntness in lying—he alone was capable of justifying what had to be done.

He is needed to fill the place waiting for him, and so, almost against his own will, despite his indecision, his lack of any plan, and all his blunders, he is drawn into a conspiracy aimed at seizing power, and the conspiracy succeeds.

He is pushed into a meeting of the legislature. In a panic he wants to flee, believing himself finished. He pretends to fall into a swoon and babbles things that should have destroyed him. But the once proud, once shrewd rulers of France, sensing that their own part is played out, are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words that would have destroyed him and kept their own power intact.

Chance—millions of chances—hand him power, and everyone acts as though by agreement to help secure that power for him. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him. Chance shapes the character of Paul I of Russia, who recognizes his government. Chance arranges a plot against him that not only fails to hurt him but ends up confirming his power. Chance puts the Duc d'Enghien in his hands and, out of nowhere, drives him to have the man killed, thereby convincing the mob, more forcefully than anything else could, that he had the right, because he had the might. Chance sees to it that although he throws all his energy into preparing an expedition against England, one that would certainly have ruined him, he never actually carries it out, but instead unexpectedly falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a fight. Chance and genius together hand him victory at Austerlitz; and by chance, everyone—not just the French but all of Europe, except England, which takes no part in the events about to unfold—despite their former horror and loathing of his crimes, now recognizes his authority, the title he has given himself, and his ideal of grandeur and glory, which suddenly strikes them all as excellent and reasonable.

As if sizing themselves up, as if rehearsing for the movement to come, the western forces push eastward again and again, in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809, gathering strength each time and growing. In 1811 the group that had formed in France merges into a single body with the peoples of Central Europe. The force of the justification behind the man at the head of this movement grows along with the size of the group. Across this ten-year period of preparation, this man has formed ties with every crowned head in Europe. The discredited rulers of the world have no reasonable ideal of their own to set against Napoleon's mad ideal of glory and grandeur. One after another they rush to parade their own insignificance before him. The King of Prussia sends his own wife to beg the great man for mercy. The Emperor of Austria counts it a favor that this man takes a daughter of the Caesars into his bed. The Pope, guardian of everything the nations hold sacred, puts religion itself to work glorifying the great man. It isn't so much Napoleon preparing himself to carry out his role, as it is everyone around him preparing him to shoulder the entire responsibility for everything that is happening and has to happen. There is no step he takes, no crime, no petty fraud, that the people around him don't instantly dress up as a great deed. The finest celebration the Germans can think up in his honor is a commemoration of Jena and Auerstädt. Not only is he great, but so are his ancestors, his brothers, his stepsons, his brothers-in-law. Everything possible is done to strip him of whatever reason he has left and to ready him for his terrible part. And by the time he is ready, so are the forces he needs.

The invasion pushes eastward and reaches its final goal, Moscow. The city is taken. The Russian army suffers heavier losses than the opposing armies suffered in the earlier fighting, from Austerlitz all the way to Wagram. But suddenly, in place of the chances and the genius that up to now had carried him, without a single break, from success to success toward his predestined goal, an endless string of chances now runs the other way, from the head cold that strikes him at Borodino to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze, to the frosts; and in place of genius, stupidity and boundless baseness come to the surface instead.
The invaders flee, turn back, flee again, and from now on all the chances run not for Napoleon but always against him.

Then a countermovement takes place from east to west, one that bears a remarkable resemblance to the movement from west to east that came before it. Attempted pushes from east to west, much like the earlier counter-movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809, come before the great westward march; there is the same coming together into a group of enormous size; the same joining of the peoples of Central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation partway through; and the same gathering speed as the goal draws near.

Paris, the final goal, is reached. The Napoleonic government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters at all; every one of his actions is now plainly pitiful and petty. And yet once again an inexplicable chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, whom they blame for their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, his crimes and his scheming laid bare, he should by rights have looked to them exactly as he had looked ten years earlier and would look again a year later: an outlaw, a brigand. But by some strange chance, no one sees him that way. His part is not finished yet. The very man who was considered an outlawed brigand ten years before, and would be considered one again a year later, is sent instead to an island two days' sail from France, an island that, for some reason, is handed over to him as his own dominion, complete with a guard of soldiers and millions of money paid to him.
